title: Lock System Business Case

opening.text: The owners will look at one security capital project this year across the region. You've asked for new locks three times. Bring me a business case I can defend to them: costs, losses, options. Hamish.

briefing: 09:30, Monday. You are Regional Director of Safety and Security. The Harbourfront's locks are fifteen-year-old magnetic stripe readers; the blank-card case showed they can be cloned and their audit trail is thin.

Veldane business case method: state the risk in evidence (incidents, losses, audits); size the expected annual loss as an average, never a worst case; set out options with whole-life costs (hardware, installation, keys, maintenance, batteries, staff time); include what each option doesn't fix; phase it if it lowers risk sooner; get engineering and front office to own their parts; take it to the decision-makers with one recommendation. Your authority is 3,000,000.

context.text: The Harbourfront charges against Vessey were dropped because the hotel's own lock log couldn't be relied on. The owners know why.

learningObjectives: Expected annual loss as an average, not a worst case
One recommendation, owned by the departments

actions.label: Pull three years of key-related losses
actions.finding: Room entries with a valid key and no forced entry, lost master keys and rekeys, guest property claims where the lock audit was inconclusive: about 26 a year across the Harbourfront, at an average cost of 2,900 each (claims, rekeys, staff time, goodwill). The blank-card case was the largest single loss, and an outlier.

actions.label: See how the current system fails
actions.findingTitle: What the old locks can't do
actions.finding: Magnetic stripe cards copy with a cheap reader; the locks keep only the last 100 entries and need a handheld to read; the encoders log to a local PC; there is no way to cancel a lost master key at the door without visiting every lock. The audit trail is too thin to rely on in court, as the Vessey case.

actions.label: Get Tomasz's view on installation and upkeep
actions.finding: Encrypted card locks fit the existing door preparations on 640 of 685 doors; 45 fire-rated doors need new hardware certified for them. Batteries every 18 months: about 20 minutes per lock, done floor by floor. He wants online locks on the back-of-house doors so he isn't walking the building for every audit.

actions.label: Cost the options with Hamish
actions.finding: A: keep the old locks, rekey as needed: no capital, losses continue. B: encrypted card locks on every door, offline, 410,000 installed, 9,000 a year in batteries and keys. C: B plus online readers and a central audit on 85 back-of-house and master-key doors, 520,000, and mobile keys later at no extra hardware. Hamish's finance view: B and C both pay back in under ten years on losses alone, before the audit and claims benefits.

lines.speaker: finance_director
lines.text: Expected loss, not the worst night you can imagine. The owners have seen enough horror stories. Give them averages they can check.

actions.label: Present the blank-card case as the yearly loss
actions.finding: The slide says the hotel 'loses up to 600,000 a year to key fraud', the blank-card case multiplied out. The owners' advisers check it against the claims history in five minutes. Every other number in the case is doubted after that.

schedules.description: The owners decline the lock project for this year: the business case 'overstated the risk by an order of magnitude'. Next year's case has to start from zero trust.

actions.label: Agree the key procedures with Gideon
actions.finding: Gideon's team owns guest key issuing on the new system: ID for every key, named encoder logins, keys cancelled at checkout and on any report of loss. He asks for training before go-live and a fallback if the encoders are down.

lines.speaker: front_office_manager
lines.text: If I own it, I want it to work at 3 a.m. with one agent on the desk. Show me that and you've got my signature.

actions.label: Present the recommendation to the owners' committee
actions.finding: Recommendation C, phased: back-of-house and master-key doors online first (the doors whose keys open everything), then the guest floors over twelve months. The owners approve 520,000 over two years with a quarterly report on key-related losses.

lines.speaker: gm
lines.text: Average losses, honest costs, and what it won't fix. That is the first business case I've seen them approve in the room.

actions.label: Write the project plan and the benefit measures
actions.finding: Phases, owners and dates; fire-rated door hardware certified; the new key procedures; and the measures: key-related losses per 1,000 room nights, master keys unaccounted for, audit trail requests answered, all reported quarterly against this year's baseline.

questions.prompt: About 26 key-related losses a year at an average of 2,900 each. What is the expected annual loss?
questions.explanation: Annualised loss = events per year x average cost = 26 x 2,900 = 75,400 a year. It is an average: some years more, some less. The blank-card case is an outlier, mentioned as such, not multiplied out.

mistakes.feedback: That is the worst case presented as the yearly loss. Expected annual loss is an average, and owners will check it.
That is one event. Multiply by how many happen in a year.

options.label: C, phased: online master-key and back-of-house doors first, guest floors over twelve months.
options.feedback: The doors whose keys open everything get a live audit first; the rest follows within the year. The highest risk falls soonest.

options.label: B: card locks everywhere, offline.
options.feedback: A real improvement, and cheaper, but master-key and back-of-house audits still mean walking to each lock.

options.label: A: keep the old locks and rekey when needed.
options.feedback: 75,400 a year in expected losses, a system that can be cloned and an audit trail that won't stand up in court.

questions.prompt: Which belong in the whole-life cost?

options.label: Locks, encoders and certified hardware for fire-rated doors
Installation, training and the fallback for encoder outages
Batteries, keys and maintenance staff time each year
The cost of the worst theft you can imagine, every year
options.feedback: That is a risk scenario, not a cost. Expected loss is an average.

questions.prompt: What should the case say the new locks won't fix?

options.label: Keys given to the wrong person at the desk, shared logins and leavers' access: procedures, not locks, fix those.
options.feedback: Saying what it won't do is what makes the rest of the case believable.

options.label: Nothing: new locks fix key security.
options.feedback: The blank-card case started with a shared login, not a lock.

options.label: Leave limitations out: they weaken the case.
options.feedback: Owners trust the case that tells them the limits.

options.label: Expected key-related loss 75,400 a year on three years' data; option C (520,000, phased: master-key and back-of-house online first) approved; front office owns key procedures; quarterly loss and audit measures against baseline.
options.feedback: The risk as an average, the decision, the owners and how benefit is measured.

options.label: Locks can be cloned; up to 600,000 a year at risk.
options.feedback: A worst case as an average. It discredits everything else.

options.label: New locks approved at 520,000.
options.feedback: The cost without the why or the how it will be judged.

checks.label: Losses from the data
checks.pass: The case starts from three years of real losses.
checks.fail: The case had no loss data.

checks.label: Average, not worst case
checks.pass: The expected loss was an average the owners could check.
checks.fail: A worst case was presented as the yearly loss.

checks.label: Engineering owns installation
checks.pass: Engineering's costs and constraints are in the case.
checks.fail: Fire-rated doors and batteries were left out.

checks.label: Front office owns keys
checks.pass: Front office signed up to the key procedures.
checks.fail: The department that issues the keys wasn't asked.

checks.label: One recommendation
checks.pass: The owners got one clear, phased recommendation.
checks.fail: The owners never saw the case.

checks.label: Measure the benefit
checks.pass: Benefits will be measured against this year's baseline.
checks.fail: Nobody will know if the locks worked.

checks.label: Show the failure
checks.pass: The weaknesses of the old system were shown, not asserted.
checks.fail: The old system's failures were never demonstrated.

debrief.whatHappened: You built a lock business case the owners approved in the room: three years of losses sized as an average, the old system's failures shown, whole-life costs with engineering and finance, what new locks won't fix, and a phased option that protects the master-key doors first.
bestPractice: Expected annual loss = events x average cost: an average, never a worst case.
Whole-life costs: hardware, installation, keys, batteries, staff time.
Phase it so the highest risk falls first.
Departments that run it own their parts; measure the benefit.
debrief.why: Owners approve cases they can check. One overstated number spends all the credibility the rest of the case earned.

lesson: Data, average loss, whole-life cost, honest limits, phased, owned and measured.
